Three ideas carry the whole of Day 1: R stores things in **objects**, you do
things with **functions**, and the commonest object is a **vector**. Run the
cells, change the numbers, break them on purpose. For the full explanation of
any of this, see [the R primer](r-primer.qmd).

## Objects

`<-` is the assignment arrow. It puts the thing on its right into the name on
its left.

```{webr}
n_students <- 240
course     <- "Community Medicine"

n_students
course
```

Change `240` to your own department's intake and run it again.

## Functions

A function is a verb. It takes arguments in brackets, separated by commas.

```{webr}
sqrt(64)
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
mean(c(72, 68, 81, 90))
```

Named arguments like `digits = 2` are clearer than positional ones. Prefer them.

## Vectors

`c()` **c**ombines values into a vector — a column of values, all of the same
type. It is the most-used function in R.

```{webr}
scores <- c(72, 68, 81, 90, 55)

scores
length(scores)
mean(scores)
```

A comparison returns a logical vector, one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per element:

```{webr}
scores <- c(72, 68, 81, 90, 55)
scores > 70
```

A vector holds **one** type. Mix them and everything is silently converted to
the most permissive type — a classic source of confusion:

```{webr}
c(1, 2, "three")
```

Those quotation marks mean all three are now text. You cannot take the mean of
that.

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: your first vector"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Five students sat an OSCE station and scored 78, 70, 91, 55 and 83.
Put those marks into a vector called `osce`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vector
osce <- ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vector
#| solution: true
osce <- c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_vector
#| check: true
target <- c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83)
if (is.character(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Those are text, not numbers. Drop the quotation marks.")
} else if (!is.numeric(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is not a numeric vector. Use c() to combine the five marks: c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83).")
} else if (length(.result) != 5) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "There should be five marks in the vector, one per student: 78, 70, 91, 55 and 83.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), target))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — that is a numeric vector of five marks.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(sort(as.numeric(.result)), sort(target)))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — all five marks are there. You have put them in a different order from the question, which is fine: these are a set of five marks, c() keeps whatever order you give it, and nothing later on this page depends on the order.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Five numbers, but not the five marks asked for. The scores were 78, 70, 91, 55 and 83.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_vector"}
`c()` combines values. The marks go inside the brackets, separated by commas.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: summarise the marks"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

How many of those five marks are 70 or above? A comparison gives you `TRUE`
and `FALSE`, and `sum()` counts `TRUE` as 1.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
osce <- c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83)

sum(______)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
#| solution: true
osce <- c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83)

sum(osce >= 70)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count
#| check: true
# The second and last check in these primers that reads your code rather than
# your answer: >= against > is the lesson here, and the value 4 alone cannot
# prove which you used. fixed = TRUE searches for those two characters as a
# literal string rather than as a regular expression, so nothing in the
# pattern can ever be read as a metacharacter.
used_ge <- any(grepl(">=", .user_code, fixed = TRUE))
value <- if (is.numeric(.result) || is.logical(.result)) as.numeric(.result) else NA_real_
if (identical(value, 4) && used_ge) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 4. Four of the five marks (78, 70, 91 and 83) are 70 or above, and your code uses >=, which is the comparison that keeps a mark of exactly 70 rather than dropping it.")
} else if (identical(value, 4)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The count is right — 4 — but the comparison is not the one you were asked for: there is no >= anywhere in your code. Several different comparisons happen to give 4 on these five marks, so the number alone does not show you counted the right thing. Count the marks that are 70 or above: sum(osce >= 70).")
} else if (identical(value, 3) && used_ge) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite — you have 3, and the answer is 4. You have used >=, so check the number you are comparing against: the bar is 70.")
} else if (identical(value, 3)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite — you have 3, and the answer is 4. There is no >= in your code, and the usual cause is > where you need >=: osce > 70 drops the student who scored exactly 70.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not the right count. osce >= 70 compares all five marks at once and gives five TRUE/FALSE values; sum() then counts the TRUEs, which should come to 4.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_count"}
You do not need a loop. `osce >= 70` compares every element at once.
:::
:::
